children: Airbus, Boeing and Embraer, the world’s largest aircraft manufacturers, agree that Africa’s air travel demand is among the fastest-growing in the world, with each seeking a bigger share of the market as airlines expand their fleets to meet rising demand.

Boeing estimates that African air traffic will grow consistently at 5.8 percent through 2045, to hit roughly 1 trillion revenue passenger kilometres (RPKs), which is total distance travelled by all paying passengers.
French manufacturer Airbus also expects a similar growth in traffic over the next two decades, with a consistent compounded annual growth rate in air traffic on African routes of 6 percent.
Brazil’s Embraer, which currently has the smallest market share in Africa, projects traffic in Africa to grow annually at 4.4 percent up to 2044, which is also among the highest globally.

These projections are consistent with those of the African Airlines Association (Afraa) and the International Air Transport Association, with the different organisations attributing it to Africa’s growing middle class and fast expanding economies.“Africa’s air travel demand is driven by a growing middle class, but to understand it with more depth, you need to look at the population of Africa. It’s a young population, increasingly urban and the GDP per household is also increasing quite well,” said Shahab Matin, Boeing’s Africa and Middle East managing director for commercial marketing.

Airbus and Embraer contend that these are the main factors that will fuel demand for air travel in Africa over the next two decades. Currently, Africa accounts for roughly just 2 percent of global air traffic, and this is set to change significantly.

With this growth, Africa is becoming a battlefront for the leading manufacturers, each projecting increased demand for new aircraft from their hangers, despite lingering financial and profitability pressures.

Airbus, for instance, sees the number of aircraft operated by African airlines more than doubling to 1,640 by 2045, with single-aisle aircraft accounting for 80 percent, as short to medium-haul routes within the continent grow significantly.“The demand within the continent is very much intra-regional and domestic transport for which the single-aisles are much more useful,” argued Joep Ellers, Airbus’s marketing director for Africa.“Another factor is that about 80 percent of intercontinental traffic coming into the continent is carried by non-African airlines, so African airlines won’t see much need for widebodies.”Boeing also sees single-aisle fleet growing significantly, with an additional 725 being added, raising the total 1,125, but projects them to hold a smaller share of about 69 percent of all aircraft on the continent.

The American manufacturer projects widebodies to rise to 315 from the current 115, accounting 20 percent of Africa’s fleet, but it sees regional jets, which it doesn’t make, diminishing from African skies, down to just 35 aircraft from 160 currently.“Routes are becoming more dense and the economies of scale of operating a larger aircraft, even if it’s just a larger narrowbody aircraft makes that a better solution in many cases,” argued Mr Matin.

Most of the growth in African traffic is expected in intra-Africa and domestic routes, which are better served by smaller, short-haul single-aisles or even much smaller regional jets which are viewed as more fuel efficient.

Embraer’s Middle East and Africa vice-president for marketing Jurjan Knol told The EastAfrican that it expects a growing demand for its regional jets on the continent, arguing that they offer similar cost per seat to narrowbodies, and are more suited for expected traffic.“The reality of today is that the vast majority of the routes that are currently flown inside Africa have a load factor below 80 percent and are operated with very few frequencies,” argued Mr Knol. “So, there is a lot of potential to increase frequencies, increase connectivity, and also improve the load factors, and airline profitability before they actually have to move up to larger narrow bodies.”Based on Embraer’s projections, the fleet of regional jets in Africa will more than double to 370 over the next 20 years, contrary to Boeing’s predictions that Africa is phasing out these jets.

However, for the African airlines expected to buy these aircraft, cost per seat or fuel efficiency may be secondary considerations. Getting the upfront capital to acquire these planes is the primary concern.

Abdérahmane Berthé, Afraa’s secretary-general, said African carriers are struggling to get financing for new aircraft acquisitions, with commercial banks pulling back amid operational challenges facing carriers.“Commercial banks see airlines and aircraft acquisition as high risk, so they are pulling back. We’re working on possible financing solutions with the Afreximbank and the AfDB,” Mr Berthé told The EastAfrican.

But he agrees that as demand grows, Boeing, Airbus and Embraer will benefit from a widening market, although new players from China, are likely to enter the market, giving the legacy firms a run for their money.

In the meantime, Boeing, Airbus, and Embraer are all working on their own initiatives of making their aircraft affordable for African carriers, through partnerships with financiers, lessors, and even governments.
